trap.wrong: "Process them in one transaction and return 200 or 500."
trap.why: One bad record fails all 10,000, a huge transaction locks tables and times out, and a retry after a timeout may duplicate everything that did commit.
trap.probe: Per-item results, idempotency, async processing for big batches, and limits.
trap.say: "Validate up front, process items independently with per-item results and an idempotency key per item, and for large batches accept the job asynchronously and report results per item when it finishes."

thesis: Bulk APIs must define partial success explicitly: per-item status and errors, per-item idempotency so retries are safe, size limits, and asynchronous processing for large batches. All-or-nothing transactions are only appropriate for small batches that must be atomic.
pitch: I'd first ask whether the batch must be atomic. Usually it doesn't: importing 10,000 contacts where 12 are invalid should import the other 9,988 and report the 12. So each item is processed independently and the response lists a status per item, with an error code and message for failures. Every item carries a client-supplied id or idempotency key so that retrying the batch, or just the failed items, doesn't duplicate successes. For large batches I'd accept the request with 202 and a job id, process it in chunks in the background, and expose progress and a per-item result file. I'd enforce limits on items per request and payload size, validate schema up front so obviously malformed batches fail fast, and rate-limit bulk endpoints separately so one import doesn't starve interactive traffic. If atomicity is truly required, keep batches small enough for a single transaction.

points.d: Most bulk operations are independent; atomic batches need small sizes and a single transaction.
Return status and error per item, in the same order or keyed by client id, so clients can retry only failures.
Client-supplied keys or external ids per item make whole-batch retries safe.
202 with a job id, chunked background processing, progress endpoint and a downloadable result.
Maximum items and bytes per request, early schema validation, clear errors for violations.
Separate rate limits and worker pools for bulk operations so imports don't hurt interactive requests.
200 with per-item results (or 207 Multi-Status) for synchronous partial success; avoid 500 when most items succeeded.

decision: Independent processing with per-item results and idempotency by default; synchronous for small batches (hundreds), asynchronous jobs for thousands or more; atomic only when the business requires it and the batch is small.
numbers: Example limits: synchronous bulk up to 500 items or 5 MB; larger batches via async jobs processed in chunks of 1,000 items.
pitfalls: One giant transaction for thousands of items.
No per-item idempotency, so retries duplicate records.
Returning only an overall status, forcing clients to guess which items failed.
Bulk jobs sharing worker pools with interactive requests.

followups.q: A client times out halfway through a synchronous bulk call. What now?
followups.a: With per-item idempotency keys they can resend the whole batch safely; already-created items return their existing result.

followups.q: Should bulk support mixed operations (create, update, delete)?
followups.a: Only if clients really need it; it complicates validation and results. Separate endpoints per operation are easier to reason about.

followups.q: How do you report results for 1 million items?
followups.a: A result file (CSV or JSON lines) in object storage linked from the job status, rather than a huge response body.

example: A CRM's import endpoint accepted up to 500 contacts synchronously with per-item results and external ids for idempotency. Larger files went through an async job returning a results file; a customer's 2-million-row import completed in 40 minutes with 3,100 rows flagged.
